hints: Start by picturing what both models agree on - where does the substrate go and what happens to the enzyme at the end of the reaction?
Now focus on the shape of the active site just before the substrate arrives - is it already a perfect match in both models, or does one model allow it to mould around the substrate?
walkthrough:
What both models share**
Think of the active site as the working part of the enzyme. In both ideas the substrate fits into the active site, an enzyme-substrate complex forms, reaction happens, product leaves and the enzyme is free to be used again. Both also explain specificity and lowering of activation energy.

Where they differ - rigid lock versus flexible glove**
In lock-and-key the active site shape is fixed and already complementary to the substrate, like a key in a lock. In induced-fit the active site is not quite the right shape at first, then it closes around and changes conformation slightly when the substrate binds, giving a better fit. That is why induced-fit can accept a slightly wider range of similar substrates.

Final answer: Similarity: in both, substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex, the enzyme is unchanged and reusable and activation energy is lowered. Difference: in lock-and-key the active site is already complementary to the substrate, whereas in induced-fit the active site is not fully complementary and changes conformation/shape to fit the substrate on binding.

hints: Recall what iodine solution looks like in the bottle before it ever meets starch - what colour would stay if no reaction happens?
walkthrough:
Remember the iodine test**
Iodine solution added to starch turns blue-black. That is the positive result. If there is no starch, there is no colour change, so the mixture simply stays the normal colour of iodine solution, which is orange-brown or amber-yellow.
Final answer: Orange / brown / amber (the colour of iodine solution, no blue-black).

hints: Look at Fig. 3.2 - absorbance rises from near 0 to 2.0 over 12 min. What does higher absorbance tell you about the amount of dark blue-black colour in the sample?
Link that colour back to Fig. 3.1 reading left to right - what substrates is phosphorylase joining together to make more of which product?
Now connect amount of product to the colorimeter - why would making more product let less light pass through?
walkthrough:
Read the trend**
Absorbance starts near 0 at 1 min and climbs steadily to 2.0 at 12 min. A higher absorbance means the sample is darker and less light gets through to the detector.

Link enzyme action to more starch**
Reading Fig. 3.1 left to right, phosphorylase adds glucose 1-phosphate to the starch chain. The extract E provides the enzyme, the added glucose 1-phosphate provides the building blocks, and the drop of dilute starch acts as a primer. As time passes, more glucose units are added so more starch accumulates.

Link starch to colour to absorbance**
When iodine is added to each sample, starch gives a blue to blue-black colour. The more starch present, the darker and more intense the colour. A darker solution absorbs more light, so the colorimeter gives a higher absorbance value. That is exactly the rising curve you see.

Final answer: Phosphorylase catalyses addition of glucose 1-phosphate to starch, so starch concentration increases with time. Iodine added to samples gives a blue / black colour with starch, darker / more intense with more starch. Darker colour transmits less light so colorimeter absorbance reading increases, as in Fig. 3.2.

hints: Look again at the double arrow in Fig. 3.1 - if you suddenly flood the right-hand side with extra phosphate ions, which direction will the reversible reaction now favour?
walkthrough:
Reverse the reaction**
Fig. 3.1 is reversible. Adding a lot of phosphate ions pushes the equilibrium to the left, the breakdown direction. Phosphorylase now removes glucose units from starch to form glucose 1-phosphate. Starch concentration falls, so the iodine test becomes paler and absorbance decreases over time.

Final answer: Added phosphate ions drive the reversible reaction in the opposite direction / to the left, so phosphorylase catalyses breakdown of starch to glucose 1-phosphate, less starch gives paler iodine colour and lower absorbance.

hints: Compare the two curves in Fig. 3.3 at every substrate concentration - which one is always lower, and where does each curve level off to its plateau?
Recall the textbook fingerprints of non-competitive inhibition - what should happen to Vmax and what should stay the same for Km when inhibitor binds away from the active site?
Pick out numbers to prove it - estimate the plateau activity with and without caffeine and check the substrate concentration needed for half Vmax in each case.
walkthrough:
Describe what you see with data**
Without caffeine the curve rises steeply to a plateau at about 190 arbitrary units from about $15 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ substrate onwards. With caffeine the curve is lower throughout, e.g. about 50 versus 75 at $5 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ and about 75 versus 150 at $10 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$, and it plateaus at only about 90 arbitrary units.

Match to non-competitive pattern**
A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a site away from the active site, changes enzyme shape and reduces functional enzyme, so Vmax falls and cannot be restored by adding more substrate. Affinity for substrate is unchanged, so Km stays the same. Competitive inhibition would keep the same Vmax, which is not seen here.

Conclude with Km evidence**
Half Vmax without caffeine is about 95, reached at roughly $6-7 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$ substrate. Half Vmax with caffeine is about 45, reached at a similar substrate concentration. Same Km plus lower Vmax plus lower plateau supports caffeine as a non-competitive inhibitor.

Final answer: Activity with caffeine is lower at all substrate concentrations and plateaus at a much lower level, so Vmax is reduced and not overcome by more substrate, e.g. about 190 arbitrary units without caffeine and about 90 units with caffeine. Km is unchanged, about same substrate concentration for half Vmax in both curves, consistent with non-competitive inhibition.
